essentials: China runs the **world's largest carbon market** by emissions covered. It started with power generation in 2021.
Since the 2025 expansion it also covers **steel, cement and aluminium smelting**; further industrial sectors are planned by 2027.
Allowances are given **free of charge against benchmarks per unit of output**. The system limits carbon intensity, not yet total emissions.
For buyers it matters through **CBAM** and through better emissions data at material suppliers.

sections.title: Why it exists
text: China has pledged to peak its carbon emissions before 2030 and reach carbon neutrality before 2060. After regional pilot markets, the national system was launched to put a price on emissions in the sectors that emit most.

sections.title: How it works
points: **Allocation**: each company receives allowances based on its output and a sector benchmark. A plant that is cleaner than the benchmark has allowances to sell; a dirtier one must buy.
**No fixed cap yet**: because allocation follows output, total emissions can grow with production. A move to absolute caps is planned.
**Compliance**: companies report emissions, have them verified and surrender allowances.
**Offsets**: certified voluntary emission reductions can cover a small share of the obligation.
**Legal basis**: State Council regulations in force since 2024 strengthened the rules and penalties for data fraud.

sections.title: Why a buyer should know it
points: **CBAM deduction**: a carbon price effectively paid in the country of origin can be deducted from the CBAM obligation, with evidence. The lower Chinese price means the deduction is small, but it exists.
**Data quality**: steel and aluminium producers under the system have verified emissions data, which your suppliers can request for product footprints.
**Cost signal**: as free allocation tightens, carbon cost will appear in material prices.

mistakes.wrong: China's carbon market caps total emissions like the EU's.
mistakes.right: It currently limits emissions per unit of output. Absolute caps are planned.

mistakes.wrong: A carbon price paid in China removes the CBAM obligation.
mistakes.right: It can be deducted, but the price is much lower than in the EU, so most of the obligation remains.

mistakes.wrong: Factories that assemble tools are covered.
mistakes.right: Only large emitters in the listed sectors are. Assemblers are affected through material and power costs.

practice: **Ask suppliers which of their material suppliers are covered** by the national carbon market.
**Request verified emissions data** for steel and aluminium where it exists.
**Keep evidence of carbon costs paid**, in case your products come into the CBAM scope.

quiz.q: How are allowances allocated in China's national carbon market?
options: Free of charge against output-based benchmarks
quiz.why: Allocation follows output and a sector benchmark, which makes it an intensity-based system.

quiz.q: Which sectors were added in the 2025 expansion?
quiz.why: These three joined power generation, which has been covered since 2021.

quiz.q: Why can total emissions still rise under the current design?
options: Because companies can leave the system
quiz.why: With output-based allocation there is no fixed total. More production means more allowances.

quiz.q: How does the Chinese carbon price interact with CBAM?
options: A carbon price effectively paid can be deducted from the CBAM obligation
quiz.why: CBAM allows deduction of a carbon price paid in the country of origin, with evidence.
